changelog.change: Initial entry — exposure types, dose units, the time-to-emesis / lymphocyte-kinetics triage, the three ARS subsyndromes, cutaneous radiation injury, external vs internal contamination management with agent-specific decorporation, and combined injury. Completes the CBRN set alongside the hazmat, incendiary, nerve-agent, and vesicant modules.

summary: A significant whole-body dose of penetrating radiation produces acute radiation syndrome — a prodrome, a latent period, then one of three dose-dependent illnesses: hematopoietic (survivable with cytokines and support), gastrointestinal (high mortality), or neurovascular (fatal). Time to vomiting and the lymphocyte count over the first 48 hours are the bedside dose estimate; contamination is a separate problem managed by removing clothing and, for internal contamination, agent-specific decorporation.
whyThisMatters: In a radiological event the immediate instinct — decontaminate before touching the patient — is backwards: life-threatening trauma is treated first, because external contamination is almost never an acute hazard to staff under universal precautions, while a delayed hemorrhage is. The dose that matters cannot be measured at the bedside for hours, so the triage tool is the clock (how fast did they vomit) and the trend (how fast are lymphocytes falling). And the treatments that change survival — early cytokines for the marrow, the right decorporation agent for the isotope, definitive surgery inside the 48-hour window — all have to start before the dose is confirmed.
clinicalTakeaway: Treat life-threatening injuries first; decontaminate after (remove all clothing — that alone removes ~90% of external contamination — then wash; save swabs and clothing for dosimetry). Record the time from exposure to first vomiting (< 1 h suggests a severe dose, > 4 h a mild one) and send serial CBC-with-differential every 6-12 h to track the lymphocyte fall. Start G-CSF (filgrastim) early for an expected significant marrow dose (roughly > 2-3 Gy or a rapidly falling count), with transfusion support, antimicrobial prophylaxis, and reverse isolation. For internal contamination, match the decorporation agent to the isotope: potassium iodide for radioiodine (only useful early), Prussian blue for cesium-137 or thallium, Ca-/Zn-DTPA for plutonium/americium/transuranics, sodium bicarbonate for uranium. Use REMM (remm.hhs.gov) and contact REAC/TS.

rows: Whole-body external irradiation
The body is in a radiation field (e.g. near an unshielded source or a detonation). Once out of the field, the person is NOT radioactive
This is what causes ARS. No decontamination needed for irradiation alone
External contamination
Radioactive material (dust, fallout) on skin, hair, clothing
Remove clothing + wash. Low acute hazard to staff with universal precautions; do not delay lifesaving care for it
Internal contamination
Radioactive material inhaled, ingested, or in a wound
Agent-specific decorporation; the dose is delivered continuously until cleared
Local high-dose exposure
A hand or body part against a strong source (industrial radiography, orphan source)
Cutaneous radiation injury — delayed, evolving burns; often no ARS

body.text: Dose is measured in gray (Gy, absorbed) or sievert (Sv, equivalent); for the photon/whole-body exposures relevant here they are numerically close. ARS becomes possible above ~0.7 Gy and is clearly symptomatic above ~1 Gy.
Bedside dose estimate — the prodrome and the lymphocytes

items: Time from exposure to first vomiting is the single most useful early triage sign: onset within 10-30 min points to a potentially lethal dose (> 4 Gy), 1-2 h to a moderate dose (2-4 Gy), > 4 h or no vomiting to a mild dose (< 2 Gy). Diarrhoea, fever, hypotension, and early erythema within hours all mark a high dose.

Absolute lymphocyte count: draw a baseline and repeat every 6-12 h. Lymphocytes fall fastest and earliest of all lineages; the rate of decline over the first 24-48 h maps to dose (the Andrews nomogram) — a count still > 1.5 ×10⁹/L at 48 h is reassuring; < 0.5 predicts severe marrow injury.

Cytogenetic biodosimetry (dicentric chromosome assay on peripheral lymphocytes) is the gold-standard dose estimate but takes days and specialised labs — send it, but triage on the prodrome and counts.
There is no useful role for a whole-body survey meter reading as a dose estimate; it detects contamination, not absorbed dose.

rows: Hematopoietic
Prodrome (hours) → latent period (days to ~3 weeks, shorter at higher dose) → pancytopenia with nadir ~day 20-30; infection and haemorrhage are the threats
Survivable with aggressive support + cytokines; LD50/60 without support ~3.5-4.5 Gy, higher with modern ICU care
Gastrointestinal

Prodrome within 1-2 h, short or absent latent period, then intractable vomiting and diarrhoea, mucosal denudation, fluid and electrolyte loss, bacterial translocation and sepsis over 1-2 weeks — overlaps with marrow failure
High mortality even with maximal support
Neurovascular (cardiovascular / CNS)
> ~10 Gy (some sources > 20-30 Gy)
Vomiting within minutes, prostration, refractory hypotension, cerebral oedema, ataxia, seizures, coma; death in 24-72 h
Uniformly fatal — comfort-focused care

body.text: Cutaneous radiation syndrome can accompany any of the above or occur alone: erythema (may appear in hours then fade and recur), epilation ~day 14-21, dry then moist desquamation, and — at high local dose — delayed ulceration and necrosis that evolves in waves over weeks to months. It is often deeper and more progressive than a thermal burn of similar early appearance.

items: Priority order: address airway, breathing, circulation, and life-threatening haemorrhage FIRST. External contamination is not an emergency for the care team under standard PPE (gown, gloves, mask, eye protection) plus a dosimeter.

Remove all clothing — this removes roughly 90% of external contamination — and bag it (labelled) for dosimetry. Then wash contaminated skin and hair with soap and lukewarm water; do not abrade the skin or use hot water (increases absorption). Cover wounds before washing surrounding skin, and irrigate contaminated wounds and eyes.
Survey with a Geiger-Müller or scintillation probe before and after decon to document and target it; aim to reduce counts to about twice background or a level that will not decrease further.
Collect nasal swabs, wound swabs, and the first 24 h of urine and faeces if internal contamination is suspected — these drive the decorporation decision and dose estimate.
Give antiemetics (5-HT3 antagonists) for the prodrome; start IV fluids and electrolyte replacement for the GI syndrome; provide analgesia for cutaneous injury.

Start a myeloid cytokine early (within ~24-72 h) when a significant marrow dose is likely — roughly > 2-3 Gy, or a lymphocyte count falling steeply: filgrastim, pegfilgrastim, or sargramostim (all FDA-approved for haematopoietic ARS). Continue until neutrophil recovery.
Thrombocytopenia: platelet transfusion for bleeding or a very low count; romiplostim is FDA-approved for haematopoietic ARS to support platelet recovery.
Transfuse leukoreduced, irradiated blood products (irradiation prevents transfusion-associated GVHD in an immunosuppressed host).

Antimicrobial prophylaxis (fluoroquinolone ± antiviral/antifungal per local protocol) during expected neutropenia; treat neutropenic fever aggressively and empirically. Reverse (protective) isolation.

Allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplant has a narrow role — a estimated dose roughly 7-10 Gy with survivable other-organ injury, no significant burns or trauma, and a donor available; outcomes historically poor.

rows: Radioiodine (I-131) — reactor accident, some RDDs
Potassium iodide (KI)
Blocks thyroid uptake. Only useful if given before or within a few hours of exposure — negligible benefit after ~24 h. Age-based dosing; greatest benefit in children and pregnancy
Cesium-137, thallium — RDD ("dirty bomb"), orphan sources
Prussian blue (insoluble ferric hexacyanoferrate)
Binds the isotope in the gut and interrupts enterohepatic recirculation; give for weeks, shortens biological half-life substantially
Plutonium, americium, curium, and other transuranics — weapons material, some industrial
Ca-DTPA then Zn-DTPA (pentetate calcium/zinc trisodium)
Chelation; Ca-DTPA is more effective initially, switch to Zn-DTPA for prolonged courses (less trace-metal depletion). IV or nebulised for inhalation
Uranium
Sodium bicarbonate
Alkalinises the urine to reduce uranyl-ion nephrotoxicity; maintain urine output. Uranium's chemical (renal) toxicity often outweighs its radiological hazard
Tritium (tritiated water)
Forced oral fluids
Dilution and increased turnover; there is no chelator

body.text: Combined injury — radiation plus trauma or burns — carries synergistic mortality: radiation impairs wound and fracture healing and the marrow dose blunts the response to infection. If surgery is needed, do the definitive procedure within the first ~48 hours (before the marrow nadir), or else delay it until haematologic recovery (around day 45 or later). Close wounds primarily when possible and minimise staged returns.

Reach-back resources: REMM (Radiation Emergency Medical Management, remm.hhs.gov) has the triage algorithms, the lymphocyte-depletion and time-to-emesis tools, and decorporation dosing. REAC/TS (Oak Ridge, 24-hour line) provides clinical consultation and biodosimetry support. State radiation control programs and the Radiation Injury Treatment Network coordinate marrow-support and transplant referral.
